subject: Specifying and fitting multi-level models with group level predictors.

messages.author: 91be17affe770359
messages.subject: Specifying and fitting multi-level models with group level predictors.
parts:
Hello stan users,
I'm struggling to fit a multi-level model with stan. I often have problems with convergence, where each chain just runs in parallel. 

I am working with soil moisture data from an observational experiment. Our experiment is set up with 8 sites in the control treatment, and 8 in the removal treatment. Each of the 16 sites contains two dataloggers, each with 4 soil moisture probes attached. We observe soil moisture at the probe level. I want to fit a model of the mean soil moisture over two days (24 hourly samples) for each probe, and the treatment effect, which is applied at the site level. 

I started with the simplest model with semi-informative priors (see pre_mean_basic.stan).
moisture ~ normal(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_moisture)
This model fit efficiently after 200 iterations. However I did not estimate probe level means, just treatment effects.

To estimate probe level means I added a layer to the model (see pre_mean_ml.stan). 
moisture[i] ~ normal(a_probe[probe[i]], sigma_moisture)
a_probe ~ N(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_probe)
This model does not fit efficiently, 400 iterations result in reasonable n_eff and Rhats for the probe level means, but not for the site level intercept or treatment slope. The traceplots show poor mixing.

I also tried recreating most of the experimental structure in the multi-level model by adding a site layer above the probe layer (see pre_mean_mls.stan).
moisture[i] ~ N(a_probe[probe[i]], sigma_moisture)
a_probe[j] ~ N(a_site[site[j]], sigma_probe)
a_site ~ N(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_site)
This model is slower to fit than the two-level model, but n_eff/N is higher for all parameters, and the traceplots show better convergence and mixing.

Is there a more efficient way to specify and fit these models? I'll use the best specification to repeatedly fit (secret weapon style) the model to each day in our time-series (~1000).


Since these are time-series data, observations are highly correlated within each probe. The nature of the correlation changes from day to day depending on rainfall. I'm not sure how to account for this in the model without introducing massive covariance matrices. Is there a more efficient method? I've considered fitting a gaussian process to the time-series within each probe to understand within day trends, but I'm not sure if that will help with the auto-correlation or not.

Thanks,
Joey

messages.author: 8aa9b8cc06fdc99c
messages.subject: Re: [stan-users] Specifying and fitting multi-level models with group level predictors.
parts:
On Mar 11, 2014, at 4:46 PM, Joey Reid <reid...@umn.edu> wrote:

> Hello stan users,
> I'm struggling to fit a multi-level model with stan. I often have problems with convergence, where each chain just runs in parallel.

> I am working with soil moisture data from an observational experiment. Our experiment is set up with 8 sites in the control treatment, and 8 in the removal treatment. Each of the 16 sites contains two dataloggers, each with 4 soil moisture probes attached. We observe soil moisture at the probe level. I want to fit a model of the mean soil moisture over two days (24 hourly samples) for each probe, and the treatment effect, which is applied at the site level.
>
> I started with the simplest model with semi-informative priors (see pre_mean_basic.stan).
> moisture ~ normal(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_moisture)
> This model fit efficiently after 200 iterations. However I did not estimate probe level means, just treatment effects.

The basic model's just a constrained linear regression with
some fairly broad priors over the constrained range. So that
shouldn't be a problem, though I don't understand the motivation
for the priors.

> To estimate probe level means I added a layer to the model (see pre_mean_ml.stan).
> moisture[i] ~ normal(a_probe[probe[i]], sigma_moisture)
> a_probe ~ N(mu_control + treatment * b_trt, sigma_probe)
> This model does not fit efficiently, 400 iterations result in reasonable n_eff and Rhats for the probe level means, but not for the site level intercept or treatment slope. The traceplots show poor mixing.

I can imagine it would give you problems given this
specification of mean:

mu_pre_pid <- mu_control + pidtrt * b_pre + sigma_pre_pid * eta_pre_pid;

given that these are all parameters:

real<lower=0,upper=1> mu_control;
real<lower=-1,upper=1> b_pre;
vector[Npid] eta_pre_pid;
real<lower=0,upper=10> sigma_pre_pid; // sd of pids

and only this is data:

vector<lower=0,upper=1>[Npid] pidtrt; // links probe to treatment

There is a serious additive non-identifiability due to
mu_control and sigma_pre_pid * eta_pre_pid, as well as
a multiplicative identifiability on sigma_pre_pid * eta_pre_pid

The choice of relatively broad priors also seems odd given that you've
constrained the parameters so tightly.

- Bob

Thanks for that, I knew I was overlooking something important. I did two things that seem to have helped a lot. First, I changed the model specification to the standard normal(mu_control + pidtrt * b_pre, sigma_pre_pid), which allowed me to drop the eta parameters, which increased speed. I still had convergence problems, so I scaled and centered the y variable (prevwc, originally a proportion [0,1]). All of the models now converge and run much faster.

Thanks again for looking at this, it was hugely helpful.

Joey
